title: Behavioral Detection Strategy for T1123 Audio Capture Across Windows, Linux, macOS
shortTitle: Behavioral Detection Strategy for T1123 Audio Capture Acr...
summary: This strategy covers T1123, Audio Capture, where an actor records microphone input to collect spoken information from meetings, calls, or a room. Detection rests on host telemetry: a process opening the microphone device that is not part of the approved conferencing or recording set, opened outside the user's normal call pattern, and sometimes paired with a new audio file written to a temporary or user directory. It fails in practice because meeting clients legitimately hold the microphone open for long periods, so the process signature, the host role, and the call context do most of the work.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for a program that turns on the microphone. Many programs do this, such as meeting applications. The rule checks which program opened the microphone and when it did so. It raises an alert when the program is not one that should record sound.
beginner.whyItMatters: A microphone can pick up private conversations and meetings. An attacker can record them without touching a camera or a screen. The recording file is small and easy to move elsewhere. Very few teams watch microphone access at all. This detection gives you a first look into that blind spot.
howItWorks: The operating system or an endpoint agent logs which process opens a microphone device.
The rule builds a list of programs that may use the microphone on each host type.
It keeps microphone opens that come from processes outside that list.
It adds context such as the account, the hour, and whether the host is a meeting room device.
It looks for a new audio file created by the same process soon afterwards.
Two or more signals together raise the alert, while a single open stays at low severity.
beginner.example: Think of a meeting room with a sign out board for the speakerphone. The board shows who borrowed it and when. The speakerphone shows as in use at two in the morning. No meeting was booked, so that entry deserves a question.
takeaways: Microphone access by an unexpected program is the core signal.
Meeting and recording software creates a lot of normal noise.
The time of day and a new audio file make an open far more suspicious.

objectives: Explain how audio capture can collect sensitive spoken information.
Identify telemetry that records which process opened a microphone device.
Build an allowlist of legitimate audio applications for each host role.
Combine microphone access with file creation and time of day to prioritise alerts.
Describe the privacy considerations that apply to monitoring microphone use.
dataSources: Endpoint detection agent records for microphone device open events with the process image and account
macOS privacy preference logs or the equivalent consent database showing microphone permission grants per application
Linux auditd or desktop environment logs recording access to the audio device files under the device directory
File creation telemetry for new audio container files, with the creating process and the destination path
logic: The pattern is a process outside the approved conferencing or recording set obtaining access to the microphone device, especially on a host that is not a designated meeting room and at a time when the user is not in a call. The fields to correlate are the process image and its signature, the account, the host role, the start and stop time of the open, and any audio file created in the same window. Benign cases are a signed meeting client holding the device for the length of a scheduled call; suspicious cases involve an unexpected parent process, a script interpreter, or a long open with no matching meeting in the calendar data.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Microphone Opened by Non Approved Process Outside Business Hours
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   service: endpoint
# detection:
#   selection:
#     EventType: 'audio_device_access'
#     Device: 'microphone'
#     AccessType: 'open'
#   filter_apps:
#     Image|endswith:
#       - '\teams.exe'
#       - '\zoom.exe'
#       - '\audacity.exe'
#   condition: selection and not filter_apps
# level: medium
falsePositives: Voice dictation and accessibility software that keeps the microphone open while the user works
Voice over internet protocol softphones and call centre clients that open the microphone for every call
Automated transcription or meeting note services that record and process scheduled meetings
Quality assurance or user research sessions that deliberately record audio with consent
Browser based meeting pages that open the microphone through the browser process instead of a dedicated client
tuningNotes: Start with an inventory of every application on the fleet that has been granted microphone access, and record an owner for each entry. Filter the approved set by signer and binary hash, and scope the rule to hosts where audio capture has no business purpose, such as servers, kiosks, and lab machines. Add business hours and calendar context as scoring signals rather than hard filters, because real meetings happen outside them. Narrowing to a fixed application list loses coverage of a legitimate meeting client abused through a malicious plug-in, so keep a separate rule for unusual child processes of meeting clients.
